summary: Trioxsalen (trimethylpsoralen) is an orally administered psoralen photosensitizer used with controlled long-wave ultraviolet A (UVA) light - photochemotherapy/PUVA - to repigment idiopathic vitiligo and to increase tolerance to sunlight in certain conditions. After ingestion and UVA exposure, it intercalates DNA and forms photo-adducts that affect epidermal cell proliferation and melanogenesis. It causes marked photosensitivity, requiring strict eye and skin protection. Note: trioxsalen is not currently an FDA-marketed product (the historical FDA brand Trisoralen has been discontinued); dosing reflects historical FDA labeling, EMA/BNF, and dermatologic PUVA practice.
indications: Repigmentation of idiopathic vitiligo (with controlled UVA exposure)
Increasing tolerance to sunlight / reducing photosensitivity reactions in selected patients

dosage.n: Do not exceed 10 mg/day; given on scheduled phototherapy days

Combined with carefully titrated UVA dose

Strictly control and measure the UVA dose; never combine with uncontrolled sun exposure

moa: A furocoumarin (psoralen) that, after photoactivation by long-wave UVA (320-400 nm), intercalates into DNA and forms covalent monofunctional and bifunctional photo-adducts with pyrimidine bases, inhibiting DNA synthesis and epidermal cell proliferation and stimulating melanocyte activity/melanin production - producing repigmentation in vitiligo.

absolute: Diseases associated with photosensitivity (e.g., lupus erythematosus, porphyria, xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism)
Melanoma or history of melanoma; invasive squamous cell carcinoma
Aphakia (absence of lens - increased retinal damage risk)
relative: Prior arsenic or ionizing radiation therapy
monitor: Skin for phototoxicity/burns and long-term skin cancer

preg: Contraindicated/avoid in pregnancy (potential mutagenic/teratogenic concern with psoralen-UVA). Use effective contraception during therapy.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding; psoralens may be excreted in milk and could photosensitize the infant.
renal: No specific renal dosing data; use with caution and standard monitoring.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; monitor liver function with prolonged photochemotherapy.

major: Other photosensitizing drugs (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, thiazides, phenothiazines, retinoids, coal tar) - additive severe phototoxicity
Concurrent UV/radiation or arsenic exposure - increased skin cancer risk
moderate: Foods/agents high in furocoumarins (lime, fig, parsley, celery, mustard) - additive photosensitivity
Hepatotoxic drugs - additive hepatic risk with prolonged use
minor: Anticoagulants - monitor with hepatic stress (limited data)
interactions.food: Take with food/milk to reduce GI upset; avoid large amounts of furocoumarin-rich foods
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive hepatic and photosensitivity risk
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate LFTs and antinuclear antibodies with prolonged use; document skin lesions for cancer surveillance

serious: Increased risk of skin cancer (squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma) with cumulative exposure

monitoring: Skin examination for phototoxicity and long-term carcinoma surveillance
Liver function tests with prolonged therapy
Cumulative UVA/PUVA dose and number of treatments
counsel: Wear UVA-protective wrap-around sunglasses for 24 hours after each dose, indoors and out
Avoid all additional sun exposure on treatment days; cover skin and use sunblock
Take with food or milk 2-4 hours before your scheduled light treatment exactly as directed
Never sunbathe or use tanning beds to enhance the effect
Report blistering, severe burns, or eye changes promptly
Long-term treatment increases skin-cancer risk - attend regular skin checks
Do not use if pregnant; avoid breastfeeding
pk: Photosensitivity develops within ~1-2 h; repigmentation over weeks-months
Short plasma half-life (~hours); first-pass hepatic metabolism
pearls: Not currently FDA-marketed - the former FDA brand Trisoralen (trioxsalen) was discontinued; dosing reflects historical FDA labeling, EMA/BNF, and dermatology PUVA practice
Trimethylpsoralen is less phototoxic than methoxsalen (8-MOP) and historically favored for oral vitiligo PUVA
Eye protection (UVA sunglasses) for 24 hours after each dose is mandatory to prevent cataracts
Cumulative PUVA increases long-term skin cancer risk - track total exposure and perform skin surveillance
Effect requires controlled UVA - never combine with uncontrolled sun exposure
missed: Trioxsalen is taken only on scheduled phototherapy days - if a dose for a treatment session is missed, skip the session and contact the dermatology team; do not take extra doses or expose to extra light to compensate.
overdose: Overdose with excessive UVA exposure causes severe phototoxic burns/blistering; oral overdose may cause GI upset. Management: keep the patient in a darkened room for 8-24 hours, treat burns as thermal injury, supportive care; protect eyes and skin. No specific antidote.
